faqs.q: What are lab-grown diamonds?
faqs.a: Lab-grown diamonds are real diamonds, created using the same carbon-crystallization process that forms diamonds underground, replicated in a controlled lab environment instead of over billions of years. They are chemically, physically, and optically identical to mined diamonds — same hardness, same brilliance, same sparkle. Every House of Seya diamond comes with IGI certification.

faqs.q: Are lab-grown diamonds real diamonds?
faqs.a: Yes. A lab-grown diamond is exactly like a natural diamond in every way that matters, except instead of being mined from the earth, it's grown in a lab. It sparkles the same, comes in the same colors and clarities, and offers the same permanence — at a fraction of the price of an equivalent mined stone.

faqs.q: Can anyone tell the difference between a lab-grown and a mined diamond?
faqs.a: No. Lab-grown diamonds share the same physical, chemical, and optical properties as natural diamonds. Even trained jewelers cannot tell them apart without specialized gemological equipment.

faqs.q: Are House of Seya's diamonds IGI certified?
faqs.a: Yes. Every diamond we set is IGI (International Gemological Institute) certified, guaranteeing cut, color, clarity, and carat weight to a globally recognized standard.

faqs.q: Do lab-grown diamonds lose their shine over time?
faqs.a: No. With a hardness of 10 on the Mohs scale, our diamonds retain their brilliance and clarity permanently, making them ideal for daily wear as well as pieces you'll treasure for years.

faqs.q: Why choose lab-grown diamonds over mined diamonds?
faqs.a: Three reasons our customers choose lab-grown: a clean, conflict-free, traceable origin; the exact same brilliance, hardness, and durability as mined diamonds; and meaningfully better value, letting you invest in a larger stone or a more intricate design without compromising your budget.

faqs.q: What is gold vermeil, and how is it different from gold plating?
faqs.a: Gold vermeil is a real, regulated jewelry standard — a rich layer of genuine gold bonded over a sterling silver base, at least 2.5 microns thick. Ordinary "gold plated" jewelry has no such minimum and is often closer to 0.5 microns, which fades within weeks. Vermeil, done properly, is built to hold its richness and durability for years.

faqs.q: How thick is House of Seya's gold vermeil, and why does that matter?
faqs.a: Our diamonds are set in 24K gold vermeil, plated at 2.5 microns — the legal international minimum for a piece to genuinely be called vermeil at all. A lot of jewelry marketed as vermeil is actually plated well below this, often around 0.5 microns, which legally only qualifies as gold plating. This means the setting around your diamond is held to a real, defensible standard, built for daily life, not just special occasions.

faqs.a: Because vermeil uses a metal base beneath the gold layer rather than gold throughout, it lets us put more of your budget toward the diamond itself — a genuine, certified stone — rather than the setting material.

blogs.title: Stop Treating Your Jewelry Like an Investment — Here's What to Do Instead
blogs.excerpt: For generations, Indian buyers have been taught to treat jewelry as an investment. Here's why that idea deserves a rethink — and how to actually protect your money while still wearing what you love.
blogs.body: For as long as most of us can remember, jewelry in India has carried a second job. It isn't just something you wear — it's something you're supposed to hold onto, protect, and eventually, if the story goes as planned, sell back for a profit.

sections.text: For as long as most of us can remember, jewelry in India has carried a second job. It isn't just something you wear — it's something you're supposed to hold onto, protect, and eventually, if the story goes as planned, sell back for a profit. Ask most Indian households why they bought a particular gold or diamond piece, and somewhere in the answer you'll hear the word “investment.”

It's such a familiar idea that we rarely stop to question it. But it's worth asking: is jewelry actually a good investment? And more importantly — is treating it like one costing you the thing jewelry was supposed to give you in the first place?
Where the “Investment” Idea Comes From

The instinct isn't irrational. For generations, gold was one of the few assets Indian households could reliably access, understand, and trust — especially at a time when formal investment options were limited, and gold jewelry doubled as both adornment and a store of value passed down through families. Buying jewelry wasn't just a purchase; it was financial planning, wrapped in something beautiful enough to wear to a wedding.

That instinct made sense in a different economic era. But holding onto it today, largely unquestioned, means a lot of jewelry — including pieces people genuinely love — ends up spending most of its life in a locker instead of on the person it was bought for.
The Real Cost of Treating Jewelry as an Investment
Here's what rarely gets talked about: jewelry is actually a poor investment vehicle, once you account for the full picture.

sections.boldText: Making charges and margins rarely come back to you.
sections.text: When you buy a piece, you're paying for the metal, the diamond or stone, and the craftsmanship that shaped it. When you sell it back, most buyers only offer you the raw material value — the gold weight, or a fraction of the diamond's worth — not what you actually paid. That gap is money that simply disappears.

sections.boldText: It sits idle, which is the opposite of what an investment should do.
sections.text: A stock, a bond, a gold ETF — these are built to be held precisely so they can grow quietly in the background while you go about your life. Jewelry can't do that. A piece sitting in a locker isn't earning anything; it's just sitting there, often insured, sometimes forgotten, doing nothing for you financially or otherwise.

sections.boldText: And the emotional cost is real too.
sections.text: Jewelry chosen for how it makes you feel — a gift, a milestone piece, something you saved up for — deserves to be worn, not treated like a financial instrument you're afraid to touch. Ask anyone who's kept a beloved piece locked away “for its value” how often they actually got to enjoy it. Usually, the honest answer is: barely at all.
Separate the Investment From the Jewelry
Here's the shift worth making: stop asking your jewelry to be your investment plan, and let it just be jewelry.

If building financial security through gold matters to you — and it's a completely reasonable goal — there are instruments built specifically for that purpose: Sovereign Gold Bonds, gold ETFs, or digital gold, all of which track gold's value transparently, without the markup of craftsmanship or the illiquidity of a physical piece. These are designed to be sold, tracked, and grown as actual financial assets.

Once your investment goals are handled separately, something freeing happens: your jewelry no longer has to justify its existence financially. You're free to choose pieces because you genuinely love them, wear them because they make you feel like yourself, and never have to weigh “how much is this worth if I need to sell it” against “how much do I love wearing this.”

That's precisely the gap House of Seya was built to sit in. When a diamond doesn't carry the enormous premium of a mined stone, and gold vermeil delivers real richness without the price of solid gold throughout, jewelry stops needing to double as a safety net. It can just be what it was always meant to be — something you choose because it's beautiful, and wear because you love it, not because you're protecting a future resale value.
You Shouldn't Have to Give Up a Piece to Get Its Value

The other part of the old model that deserves rethinking: the idea that the only way to ever “realize” value from a piece is to give it up entirely — melt it down, sell it back for a fraction of what you paid, and lose it forever.

That's part of why we built our Lifetime Buyback Program the way we did. It exists as a safety net for the pieces you no longer wear, not as the reason you bought them in the first place. Your jewelry doesn't have to earn its keep by sitting untouched — you can wear it constantly, love it fully, and know that if your taste changes down the line, there's still a path to real value without having started from a place of financial anxiety about a piece you were supposed to be enjoying.
Wear It. That Was the Whole Point.

Jewelry was never meant to be a locker's most frequent visitor. It was meant to catch the light at dinner, sit at your collarbone on an ordinary Tuesday, and make you feel a little more like yourself every time you put it on.
Put your investment goals where they belong — in instruments built for growth. And put your jewelry where it belongs too: on you.

whatAreLabGrown.title: What Are Lab-Grown Diamonds?
whatAreLabGrown.p1: Lab-grown diamonds are real diamonds — not imitations, and not a separate category of gemstone. They're created using one of two established methods, CVD (Chemical Vapour Deposition — A standard at HOS) or HPHT (High Pressure High Temperature), which replicate the exact natural process that forms diamonds underground, just inside a controlled lab environment instead of the earth's crust over billions of years.
whatAreLabGrown.p2: The result is a stone that is chemically, physically, and optically identical to a mined diamond: the same carbon crystal structure, the same hardness, the same brilliance and fire. Every House of Seya diamond is IGI certified, so that identity is independently documented, not just claimed.

fourCs.title: THE 4C'S OF DIAMONDS
fourCs.intro: Every diamond, lab-grown or mined, is evaluated on the same four characteristics. Understanding them is the single most useful thing you can do before buying.

items.title: Cut
items.body: Cut is the most important of the 4Cs, and the one most buyers underweight. It refers to how well a diamond's facets interact with light — a well-cut diamond reflects light back through the top of the stone, creating the brilliance and sparkle diamonds are prized for. A poorly cut diamond can look dull even with excellent color and clarity. For the best balance of beauty and value, look for an Excellent or Very Good cut grade.

items.title: Colour
items.body: Colour measures how close to colourless a white diamond is, graded on a scale from D (completely colourless) to Z (noticeably tinted). The closer to D, the rarer and more valuable the stone. Most buyers find the best value in the G–H range, where any warmth is essentially invisible to the naked eye but the price is meaningfully lower than a D-E-F stone.

items.title: Clarity
items.body: Clarity measures internal inclusions and external blemishes — natural characteristics formed during the diamond's growth. Grades range from Flawless (extremely rare) down to Included (visible inclusions to the naked eye). VS1–VS2 and SI1 grades typically offer inclusions invisible without magnification, making them the sweet spot for value-conscious buyers.

items.title: Carat
items.body: Carat measures a diamond's weight, not its size directly — though the two are closely related. One carat equals 200 milligrams. Because larger diamonds are rarer, price increases disproportionately as carat weight goes up. A well-cut diamond can also appear larger than its carat weight suggests, which is part of why cut quality matters more than raw size.

certification.title: Understanding IGI Certification
certification.p1: A diamond certificate is effectively an identity document for your stone. It's issued by an independent gemological laboratory — not the jeweler selling the diamond — after the stone has been examined and graded under controlled conditions. This independence is what makes a certificate meaningful: it's a second, unbiased opinion on exactly what you're buying.
certification.p2: House of Seya diamonds are certified by IGI (International Gemological Institute), one of the world's most widely recognized and trusted grading authorities.

certification.concluding: Every House of Seya diamond ships with its IGI certificate. It's not an optional upgrade — it's how we make sure you never have to simply take our word for what you're buying.

items.text: Prioritising carat size over cut quality — a smaller, well-cut diamond will often out-sparkle a larger, poorly cut one.
Buying without a certificate, or accepting a certificate from an unfamiliar, non-independent lab.
Assuming all diamonds within a grade look identical — cut quality and fluorescence can meaningfully affect appearance even within the same clarity or colour grade.
Not asking whether the stone is lab-grown or mined — reputable sellers should always disclose this clearly, not leave it ambiguous.

items.reality: A lab-grown diamond is exactly as real as a mined one — same carbon structure, same hardness, same optical properties. The only difference is where it was created.

items.myth: You can tell a lab-grown diamond apart with the naked eye.
items.reality: You cannot. Even trained gemologists need specialized equipment, like spectroscopy, to distinguish origin — visual inspection alone isn't enough.

items.myth: Lab-grown diamonds won't hold up over time.
items.reality: With a hardness of 10 on the Mohs scale — the same as natural diamonds — lab-grown diamonds are exceptionally durable and are not more prone to damage or dulling with age.

items.myth: Certification doesn't matter for lab-grown diamonds.
items.reality: If anything, certification matters just as much. It's the only independent confirmation of the exact cut, colour, clarity, and carat weight you're paying for, regardless of origin.

faqs.q: Are lab-grown diamonds graded on the same scale as natural diamonds?
faqs.a: Yes. Lab-grown diamonds are graded using the same 4Cs — cut, colour, clarity, and carat weight — as natural diamonds. At House of Seya, every diamond comes with full IGI grading documentation for complete transparency.

faqs.q: Do lab-grown diamonds lose their shine over time?
faqs.a: No. Lab-grown diamonds retain their brilliance and clarity permanently. With a hardness of 10 on the Mohs scale, they're extremely durable and suitable for daily wear as well as pieces meant to last a lifetime.

faqs.q: How much more affordable are lab-grown diamonds than mined diamonds?
faqs.a: Generally, lab-grown diamonds offer meaningfully better value for the same size and quality, since the supply chain avoids the costs associated with mining, exploration, and distribution of natural stones.

faqs.q: What's the difference between CVD and HPHT lab-grown diamonds?
faqs.a: Both are legitimate methods of growing diamonds in a lab. CVD (Chemical Vapour Deposition) grows a diamond layer by layer from a carbon-rich gas. HPHT (High Pressure High Temperature) replicates the natural underground conditions using extreme pressure and heat. Both produce chemically identical, real diamonds.

faqs.q: Why does IGI certification matter if I trust the brand I'm buying from?
faqs.a: Because a certificate is independent of the seller. It's issued by a third-party gemological lab with no stake in the sale, so it protects you even if your assessment of the brand later changes. It's documentation you keep, not just a claim you were told.
